evidence.text:
Homogeneous Catalysis
Chromium-Catalyzed Selective Dimerization/Hydroboration of
Allenes to Access Boryl-Functionalized Skipped ( E,Z)-Dienes
Yinsong Zhao and Shaozhong Ge*
Abstract: A chromium-catalyzed dimerization/hydroboration
of allenes is developed to access synthetically versatile boryl-
functionalized skipped dienes with a catalyst generated in situ
from CrCl2 and a pyridine-2,6-diimine ligand mesPDI. A variety
of allenes reacted with pinacolborane (HBpin) to afford the
corresponding boryl-functionalized (E,Z)-1,4-dienes in high
yields and with excellent selectivity. Electron paramagnetic
resonance (EPR) spectroscopic studies suggest that this
chromium-catalyzed reaction probably proceeds through
a chromium(I) hydride intermediate.
Catalysts based on first-row transition metals, such as iron,
cobalt, nickel, and copper, have been extensively studied in
reaction discovery and development over past decades
partially because of their low price, high abundance, and
low toxicity.
[1] Chromium, a first-row early transition metal in
Group 6, is an abundant element in the Earth/C29s crust.
Although Cr
VI compounds are highly toxic, Cr II and Cr III
compounds, such as CrCl 2 and CrCl 3, have low toxicity. [2]
Chromium compounds have shown unique catalytic reactiv-
ities in Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi reactions,
[3] various cross-
coupling reactions, [4] and the polymerization and oligomeri-
zation of olefins. [5] However, chromium-catalyzed hydrobo-
ration reactions of unsaturated hydrocarbons that can afford
synthetically versatile organoboron compounds
[6] have
remained unknown.
Skipped dienes are valuable structural motifs in numerous
bioactive natural products and synthetic compounds (Sche-
me 1 A).[7] Several synthetic approaches, such as hydroallyla-
tion of alkynes, [8] hydroalkenylation of 1,3-dienes, [9] and
coupling of vinyl metallic reagents with various allylic
electrophiles,
[10] have been developed to prepare skipped
dienes. However, systematic approaches to access boryl-
functionalized skipped dienes from readily accessible starting
materials are still lacking. Considering broad applications of
organoboron compounds in chemical synthesis,
[6] we are
interested in developing selective approaches to synthesize
boryl-functionalized skipped dienes because they can be
further converted to other unsaturated hydrocarbons via
selective C/C0B bond transformations.
Allenes are polyenes containing two cumulative carbon-
carbon double bonds, and they can undergo dimerization or
trimerization in the presence of transition-metal catalysts.
[11]
Therefore, we envisioned that a reaction between an allene
and HBpin with a stoichiometry of 2:1 would afford a boryl-
functionalized diene, provided that a catalyst could be
identified to catalyze sequential dimerization and hydro-
boration of allenes. Catalytic hydroboration of allenes has
been well studied with various metal catalysts to prepare
allylic or alkenyl boronates.
[12] Nevertheless, none of these
catalysts have been shown to promote dimerization of allenes
during hydroboration reactions. There is one example of
a borane-mediated dimerization of arylallenes reported by
Erker (Scheme 1 B),
[13] and this stoichiometric reaction
employs a highly reactive and electrophilic hydroborane
(C6F5)2BH and affords a boryl-functionalized ( E,E)-1,5-diene
product.
During our recent studies on cobalt-catalyzed hydro-
functionalization of allenes, [12d, 14] we became interested in
exploring other base metal catalysts for the reactions of
allenes with pinacolborane (HBpin), with the aim of discov-
ering new selectivity. Herein, we report the first selective
chromium-catalyzed dimerization/hydroboration of allenes
with HBpin to prepare boryl-functionalized skipped ( E,Z)-
dienes (Scheme 1 C). We also show that these boryl-contain-
ing ( E,Z)-1,4-diene products can be converted to various
stereo-defined alkenyl compounds by standard functional
group interconversions. Furthermore, preliminary mechanis-
tic studies including deuterium-labeling and electron para-
magnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopic experiments sug-
gest that this chromium-catalyzed dimerization/hydrobora-
Scheme 1. Boryl-functionalized skipped dienes generated by coupling
of two allenes with boron reagents.

mediate.
We initiated our studies on dimerization/hydroboration of
allenes by identifying a selective catalyst and reaction
conditions for hydroboration of allene 1a with HBpin to
yield the 1,4-diene product 2a (Table 1). After systematic
evaluations of various first row metal catalysts (entry 12 in
Table 1) and other reaction parameters, we found that the
reaction conducted with the catalyst generated from CrCl
2
and a pyridine-2,6-diimine ligand mesPDI ( L1) afforded the
desired product 2a in 78 % isolated yield (entry 1 in T able 1).
The reaction did not occur in the absence of CrCl 2 (entry 2 in
Table 1), ligand L1 (entry 3 in T able 1), or the activator
NaBHEt3 (entry 4 in Table 1). We also tested other PDI
ligands L2-L7 for this transformation, but these reactions
produced 2a either in decreased yields (entries 5 and 6 in
Table 1) or only in trace amounts (entries 7 and 8 in T able 1).
The catalyst generated from CrCl 3 and L1 was also active for
this transformation (entry 9 in Table 1). We also tested other
activating reagents for this reaction. For example, the reaction
run with EtMgBr occurred to complete conversion of 1a , but
the yield of 2a for this reaction is slightly decreased when
compared with the reaction conducted with NaBHEt
3 (64 %;
entry 10 in Table 1). The reactions run with NaH, magnesium,
or zinc as activators did not take place (entry 11 in T able 1).
With the optimized reaction condition in hand (entry 1 in
Table 1), the scope of allenes was investigated (Table 2).
Generally, a variety of alkyl- and aryl-substituted allenes
reacted with HBpin in the presence of 3 mol % CrCl
2/mesPDI
and 6 mol % NaBHEt 3, affording the corresponding boryl-
containing skipped ( E,Z)-dienes ( 2a -2z ) in modest to high
isolated yields (52 %-87 %). This Cr-catalyzed transformation
shows good functional group tolerance, and various reactive
groups, such as ether (2g -2k ), fluoro (2d ), chloro (2g and 2z ),
bromo (2e, 2h , and 2k ), acetal ( 2j ), tosylate ( 2q ), silyl ether
(2r and 2s ), terminal alkene ( 2i and 2t ), and thioether ( 2y )
moieties are compatible with the reaction conditions. Fur-
thermore, silyl-substituted and heteroaryl-containing allenes
also reacted to afford the corresponding dienes 2o and 2v in
good isolated yields, respectively. However, allenes contain-
ing ketone or aldehyde groups do not undergo this Cr-
catalyzed transformation. Furthermore, we also conducted
a gram-scale reaction with allene 1p (6.00 mmol), and this
reaction afforded the diene product 2p (1.03 g) in 72 %
isolated yield.
We then explored Cr-catalyzed dimerization/hydrobora-
tion with two different allenes. Initial attempts on the

reactions employing two allenes with equal molar ratio
showed that cross-dimerization/hydroboration products did
not form with noticeable selectivity. However, increasing the
molar ratio of two allenes to 1:2 led to an increased selectivity
that allows effective purification of cross-dimerization/hydro-
boration products. The selected examples of cross-dimeriza-
tion/hydroboration reactions are given in Equation (1), and
these reactions afforded the desired diene products with good
selectivity (with the ratios of products from cross- and homo-
dimerization/hydroboration varying from 6:1 to 15:1), albeit
in modest isolated yields.
To demonstrate the synthetic utility of this chromium-
catalyzed dimerization/hydroboration procotol, we con-
ducted various synthetic transformations with the boryl-
functionalized diene products 2b and 2p, and these reactions
are summarized in Scheme 2. Compound 2p could be readily
oxidized by NaBO
3, affording allylic alcohol 4 in 95 %
isolated yield (Scheme 2 A). Epoxidation of compound 4
with m-CPBA occurred selectively on the trisubstituted
alkene unit to produce epoxide 5 in 72 % yield (Scheme 2 B).
Allylic boronate 2p could undergo hydroxymethylation with
paraformaldehyde to afford homoallylic alcohol 6, which
could be converted to compound 7 selectively in high yield via
cobalt-catalyzed cyclopropanation of alkenes (Sche-
me 2 C,D).
[15] Compound 2p also underwent aminomethyla-
tion to produce homoallylic amine 8 in 86 % yield (Sche-
me 2 E).[16] Furthermore, we also showed that diene product
2b could undergo NiH-catalyzed remote hydroarylation with
aryl iodides in the presence of (EtO) 3SiH to give allylic
boronates 9 and 10 in good isolated yields (Scheme 2 F). [17]
To provide insights into the nature of the active chromium
species for this reaction, we conducted electron paramagnetic
resonance (EPR) spectroscopic studies on the chromium
catalyst (Figure 1). No EPR signals were observed for the
mixture of CrCl
2 and mesPDI ligand with a molar ratio of 1:1.
However, upon addition of 2 equiv of NaBHEt 3 to the
mixture of CrCl 2 and mesPDI, a singlet resonance appeared
with a g value of 2.001 (Figure 1 A), which is consistent with
the value observed for Cr I species.[5f] We then monitored by
EPR spectroscopy the reaction of allene 1a with HBpin
catalyzed by CrCl 2/mesPDI in the presence of NaBHEt 3
(entry 1 in Table 1), and observed a singlet resonance with
a g value of 1.998 (Figure 1 B). A similar singlet resonance
with a g value of 1.999 was observed for the corresponding
dimerization/hydroboration reaction catalyzed by CrCl
3/
mesPDI (entry 9 in Table 1). The results of these EPR
spectroscopic studies suggest that Cr I intermediates are
likely the active species in this Cr-catalyzed transformation.
We subsequently conducted some control experiments to
get more information about the active chromium intermedi-
ates. Previous studies showed that PDI-ligated CrCl 2 could be
reduced to PDI-ligated CrCl compound by NaH. [5e] However,
the reaction of allene 1a with HBpin catalyzed by CrCl 2/
mesPDI in the presence of NaH did not proceed (entry 11 in
Table 1), probably because of sluggish activation of the
catalyst precursor by NaH. We then carried out this reaction
with preformed (
mesPDI)CrCl, and this reaction still did not
occur [Eq. (2)]. However, the combination of ( mesPDI)CrCl
and 1.2 equivalents of NaBHEt 3 was active for dimerization/
hydroboration of allene 1a [Eq. (2)]. We then conducted
EPR spectroscopic analysis on the reaction catalyzed by
(
mesPDI)CrCl and NaBHEt3, and observed a singlet resonance
with a g value of 1.998 (Supporting Information, Figure S5),
which is the same with the resonance shown in Figure 1 B.
Furthermore, we also performed a deuterium-labeling experi-
ment for the reaction of allene 1p with DBpin under standard

conditions [Eq. (3)]. This reaction afforded compound 2p -d1
in 74 % yield, and the deuterium atom was selectively
incorporated onto the ( Z)-alkenyl carbon. These results
suggest that a Cr I/C0H species is likely the active chromium
intermediate of this dimerization/hydroboration reaction.
We also found that this chromium-catalyzed dimerization/
hydroboration of allenes showed profound solvent effects
(Scheme 3 A). For example, the reaction between cyclohexyl-
substituted allene 1n and HBpin proceeded to full conversion
of 1n and yielded the desired boryl-containing skipped diene
2n in high yields (74–95 %, Scheme 3 A) when these reactions
were conducted in solvents with high coordinating ability,
such as THF , 1,4-dioxane, and dimethoxyethane. However,
the corresponding reactions conducted in non-coordinating
solvents, such as toluene and hexane, did not take place
(Scheme 3 A). We subsequently monitored by EPR spectros-
copy the reaction of allene 1n with HBpin catalyzed by
3 mol % of CrCl
2/mesPDI in toluene and the EPR spectrum
showed a very weak signal with a g-value of 2.004 (Sche-
me 3 B). However, the addition of 0.5 equivalent of THF ,
relative to allene 1n , to the reaction mixture promoted the
formation of a significant amount of active chromium species
(Scheme 3 C). Accordingly, the reaction of allene 1n with
HBpin catalyzed by 3 mol % of CrCl
2/mesPDI in toluene also
proceeded to full conversion of 1n and afforded the desired
product in 92 % GC yield when 50 mol % THF was added
(Scheme 3 D). To account for these observed solvent effects,
we rationalized that coordinating solvents might help to
solvate CrCl
2 and act as a ligand to stabilize the sterically and
electronically unsaturated Cr I species.
The kinetic behavior of this chromium-catalyzed dimeri-
zation/hydroboration of allenes was assessed by conducting
kinetic studies on the reaction of cyclohexyl-substituted
allene 1n with HBpin catalyzed by CrCl
2 and mesPDI in
THF at room temperature (Supporting Information, Fig-
ure S8). The plots of the initial rates of the reaction vs. the
concentration of the catalyst, allene 1n , and HBpin are shown
in the Supporting Information, Figures S9–S11. The results of
these kinetic studies showed that this chromium-catalyzed
dimerization/hydroboration of allene is first order in chro-
mium catalyst and zero order in allene and HBpin.
Based on the results of EPR spectroscopic analysis,
control experiments, solvent effects, and kinetic studies, we
proposed a catalytic cycle depicted in Scheme 4 for this
chromium-catalyzed dimerization/hydroboration of allenes.
The activation of CrCl
2 with NaBHEt 3 in the presence of
mesPDI in THF generates a Cr I hydride ( L)(THF)2Cr/C0H( I).
Dissociation of a THF molecule from the chromium inter-
mediate I forms a sterically and electronically unsaturated Cr I
hydride species ( L)(THF)Cr/C0H( II). Allene 1 then coordi-
nates with (L)(THF)Cr/C0H followed by migratory insertion to
generate an allylchromium intermediate ( IV).[18] Subsequent
reactions of allene 1 with allylchromium species ( IV) via
coordination and insertion form a C /C0C bond between two
allene molecules and generate a new allylchromium species
(VI).[19] The intramolecular coordination of the cis-C=C bond
in this chromium intermediate might inhibit its further
migratory insertion reactions with allenes. In the last step,
intermediate VI reacts with HBpin in THF to afford product 2
and regenerate Cr
I hydride species ( L)(THF)2Cr/C0H. In the
chromium intermediates (III) and (V), the allene coordinates
with chromium catalysts in a way that the substituent R points
away from the catalysts to minimize the steric repulsion,
which explains the stereochemistry of the two double bonds in
the skipped ( E,Z)-diene product 2. The observed first order

rate dependence on the concentration of the chromium
catalyst and zero order rate-dependence on the concentra-
tions of allene and HBpin indicate that the dissociation of
THF from (L)(THF)

the turnover-limiting step for this dimerization/hydroboration
process.
In summary, we have developed an effective protocol to
prepare boryl-functionalized skipped ( E,Z)-1,4-dienes via
selective chromium-catalyzed dimerization/hydroboration of
allenes. V arious terminal allenes reacted with HBpin to
produce the corresponding boryl-containing skipped dienes in
high yields with excellent regio-, chemo-, and stereoselectiv-
ity. This reaction provides a versatile access to series of stereo-
defined alkenyl and skipped dienyl compounds. Preliminary
mechanistic studies suggest that this chromium-catalyzed
dimerization/hydroboration occurs through a Cr
I/C0H inter-
mediate. Studies to determine the detailed mechanism of this
transformation and to develop chromium-catalyzed hydro-
functionalization of other types of unsaturated hydrocarbons
will be the subjects of future work.
